transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. It’s... well, to be completely honest, it feels a bit silly even saying it out loud. My daughter is actually the one who pushed me to make the appointment because I’ve been so, well, just so preoccupied lately. You see, I’ve been a bookkeeper for going on forty years now—mostly for a local hardware distributor, just keeping the ledgers balanced and all that, so my hands are always right out there on the desk, you know? 

And... well, a little while back, I had a clumsy moment in the kitchen and ended up with this scar on my left wrist. I know... logically, I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. The doctor who stitched it up said it healed beautifully. But I just can't seem to let it go. When I’m out and about, especially when I’m at church on Sunday mornings, or when I sit down for my Tuesday bridge club with the girls—we’ve been playing together since the late nineties, mind you—I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. 

It’s like it’s the very first thing they notice about me now. I find myself constantly pulling my cardigan sleeves down, even if the fellowship hall is warm, or hiding my hand under my purse on the card table, because I just feel this heavy spotlight on my wrist. It completely distracts me from the sermon, or the game, and I just end up talking myself in circles about it, worrying about what they're thinking. Even though part of my brain says I'm making a mountain out of a molehill, I just can't seem to turn off that awful feeling that they're all staring at it.
Has this preoccupation with your wrist scar been affecting your work as a bookkeeper?

Well, yes, actually, it really has been. And that’s something that bothers me to no end, because, like I said, I’ve been doing this for forty years, and I’ve always prided myself on being punctual. You know, Mr. Henderson—he’s the owner of the hardware distributor—he always used to say you could set your watch by my monthly reports. But lately... oh, it’s just been so frustrating. I’ll sit down at my desk with the ledgers, and I’ll catch a glimpse of my wrist, and suddenly I’m spending twenty minutes just adjusting my cuffs, trying to find a way to position my arm so the scar doesn’t show when I’m typing or writing. And before I know it, half the morning is gone, and I’m scrambling. I’ve actually been late turning in my work the past few weeks, which is just so unlike me. I hate making excuses to Mr. Henderson, but I can't exactly tell him I was too busy fussing over my sleeves, can I? 

And it’s not just work, either. It’s bleeding into the things I actually enjoy doing. I’ve been volunteering with the church choir for ages—I don’t sing much anymore, but I help organize the sheet music and the robes—and I also help out front-of-house for the community theater downtown. Just taking tickets and handing out programs, that sort of thing. But I’ve skipped some of my commitments there recently. I just... I get so caught up in front of the mirror before I leave the house, trying on different bracelets, different long-sleeved blouses, just doing everything I can to make absolutely sure my wrist won’t be noticed by anyone I’m handing a program to or passing music to. And if I can't get it to look right, if I can't hide it well enough, I just call in and say I’m not feeling well. Which makes me feel terribly guilty, because they rely on me, but the thought of standing there with everyone staring at my hand... I just can't do it.
Have you started to worry about how other parts of your body or face look to others, not just the scar on your wrist?

Oh, no, no, nothing like that. It's really just the wrist. I mean, goodness, at my age—sixty-four—you sort of make peace with the wrinkles and the gray hairs, don't you? I stopped coloring my hair, oh, it must be five years ago now. My daughter told me I should let the silver grow in, and I did, and I don't give it a second thought. And my face, well, it's just my face. It's the same one I've been looking at in the mirror for decades, just a little more weathered. 

I've never been one of those women who spends hours fussing over makeup or worrying about a little extra weight around the middle. I mean, my husband, God rest his soul, he always said I looked fine just the way I was, and I believed him. So, no, I don't sit around analyzing my nose or my chin or anything like that. If I get a blemish, well, I just put a little concealer on it and go about my day. 

It really is just this... this awful scar. It’s so out of place. It just doesn't belong there, right on my wrist where everyone can see it when I'm handing them a bulletin or pointing to a line in the ledger. It’s like a neon sign. But the rest of me? No, I’m perfectly fine with the rest of me. It’s just this one terrible mistake in the kitchen that I can't seem to stop fixating on. If I could just get my wrist back to normal, I wouldn't have a care in the world about how I look.
Have you noticed any difficulty in forming or maintaining relationships with others due to your concerns about the scar?

Oh, goodness, no, I wouldn't say that at all. My friends and my family, they’re just wonderful, they really are. I mean, like I mentioned with my Tuesday bridge club—that’s Mary, Susan, and Linda—we’ve been thick as thieves for over twenty years now. And they haven't treated me any differently, not one bit. Even though I sit there and I just *know* my sleeve is riding up, and I feel my face getting hot because I’m so worried they’re staring at the scar... they never say a word about it. They just keep right on talking about Susan’s grandchildren or the new landscaping down at the community center. 

And my daughter, well, she’s the one who made this appointment for me, bless her heart. We talk on the phone every single evening, usually right after she finishes making dinner for her boys. We're as close as we've ever been. I suppose... well, I suppose the relationships themselves are perfectly fine. It’s just me getting in my own way, isn't it? Because I haven't lost any friends, and I still chat with the folks at church when I run into them at the grocery store—I always seem to bump into someone from the choir when I’m picking up my produce on Thursday mornings, and we always have a lovely catch-up right there in the aisle. 

So, no, they haven't pulled away from me, and I certainly haven't stopped caring for them. It’s just this terrible distraction I get when I’m *with* them, feeling like this... this mark on my wrist is all they can see. But they still invite me to everything, and Mary even brought over a lovely baked ziti just last week when I was feeling a bit too overwhelmed to cook. So, thank the Lord, my friendships are completely intact. I don't know what I'd do without my girls, especially since my husband passed. They really are a lifeline, so I make absolutely sure to keep up with them, even if I have to spend an extra twenty minutes picking out the right long-sleeved sweater before they come over.
Have you felt like your concerns about the scar have taken over your life to the point where you feel like you're no longer yourself?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say it's taken over my life, not completely. I mean, I'm still me, you know? I'm still the same person who loves a good game of bridge and enjoys organizing the sheet music at church, even if I have been missing a few days here and there. I still make my morning coffee exactly the same way—half a teaspoon of sugar, a splash of skim milk—and I still sit out on the porch when the weather is nice to read the morning paper. My husband and I used to do that every morning, rain or shine, and I've kept up the tradition. So, no, I don't feel like I've lost myself or anything drastic like that. 

It's more like... it's just this incredibly annoying, persistent little gnat buzzing around my head, if that makes sense. It's a distraction. A very frustrating, time-consuming distraction that makes me late for work and makes me fuss over my sweaters. But at the end of the day, when I'm sitting in my favorite armchair watching the evening news, I'm still just me. I haven't turned into a completely different person or anything. I just... I just have this one thing that I can't seem to stop worrying about. But it hasn't, you know, erased who I am. I'm still the same old bookkeeper who loves her daughter and her friends, just... a bookkeeper who spends a little too much time adjusting her cuffs nowadays.
Do you feel like your worry about the scar is causing you significant distress?

Significant distress? Oh, goodness, 'distress' is a very strong word, don't you think? When I hear the word distress, I think of... well, I think of when my husband had his heart attack. Now *that* was distress. Or even just... oh, do you remember when we had that awful storm back in 2018 and the basement at the church flooded right before the Easter service? I was doing the bookkeeping for the parish then, still am of course, but we had to figure out how to pay for the water damage and replace all the choir robes and the folding chairs. That caused me absolute sleepless nights. That was distress. 

But this? The scar? It's really just... it's highly irritating. It's a bother. I mean, yes, I get a little flustered, say, when I'm at the grocery store and I reach up to the top shelf for a can of crushed tomatoes—I always buy the San Marzano ones for my baked ziti, my daughter insists they make a difference because they're less acidic, and she really is right about that—and as I reach up, I feel my sleeve slide down. I get a hot flash of embarrassment, surely, because I just know someone might catch a glimpse of it right there in aisle four. But I wouldn't say I'm in *distress*. I don't go home and cry into my pillow or pull the covers over my head. I just tug the sleeve back down, make sure it's secure, and move right along to the produce section to pick out my iceberg lettuce. 

It's more of a constant, nagging frustration than anything else. Like... oh, like a pebble in your shoe that you just can't quite shake out, no matter how many times you take the shoe off and bang it against the pavement. It's always there, and you're always aware of it, and it makes you walk a little funny, but you still get to where you're going. So, no, I wouldn't use a phrase like significant distress. Just a very, very persistent annoyance that I wish I could magically erase so I wouldn't have to spend quite so much time agonizing over the cuffs of my cardigans every single morning.
Does this worry about your scar happen to you every day?

Every day? Oh, yes, I suppose it really is every single day. It’s hard to avoid, you see, because you use your hands and your arms for absolutely everything. From the moment I wake up and pour that first cup of coffee to when I’m shuffling invoices at my desk for the parish bookkeeping... it’s just always right there in my line of sight. 

And the funny thing is—and I do realize this, I really do—I know the scar on my wrist is probably not nearly as bad as it looks to me. Logically, I know it’s just a mark. It’s not the end of the world, and I'm sure most people have a blemish or two. But my goodness, when I’m out and about, it just feels like it’s glowing in the dark or something. Like when I’m at church on Sunday mornings, reaching out to hand someone a hymnal, or when I’m sitting at the card table for bridge on Tuesdays... I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right straight to it. It’s the most unsettling feeling. I’ll be sitting there dealing the cards to Mary and Linda, and I’ll just think, 'They’re looking at it, they’re all looking at my wrist.' 

It just feels like it’s the very first thing they notice about me now. Not my smile, not my new glasses, not even the fact that I brought the good shortbread cookies from that little bakery down on Main Street, but just... that scar. So, yes, because I’m around people every day, or at least running errands and going about my normal routine, the worry is just always sitting there with me, every single day, without fail.
Have you had to avoid any important activities or events because of your concerns about the scar?

Well, I wouldn't say I've avoided anything *important*, like a wedding or a funeral, but... well, yes, I suppose it has gotten in the way of a few things lately. It’s embarrassing to admit, really, because I pride myself on being reliable. I’ve been doing the bookkeeping for the parish for nearly fifteen years, and I’ve always been the one you can count on to have the monthly reports perfectly balanced and turned in by the third of the month. Always. But... well, this past month, I was actually a few days late handing in the ledgers. And it wasn't because the math was tricky or because we had unexpected expenses. It was because I spent so much time in the mornings just standing in front of my closet, trying on different sweaters and blouses, twisting my arm this way and that in the mirror, trying to find a combination where the cuff would stay put and cover my wrist completely. By the time I finally felt secure enough to leave the house, I was already behind schedule, and it just snowballed.

And then there's the volunteering. I've always loved helping out with the church choir—organizing the sheet music, making sure the robes are pressed, that sort of thing. And the local community theater, too! I usually help them with their ticket sales and the front-of-house organization during their spring musical. They’re doing *The Music Man* this year, which is just my absolute favorite, I know all the songs by heart. But... I’ve actually skipped a few of my scheduled volunteer days for both of those recently. I just... I get so worked up thinking about being in those crowded rooms, handing out programs or passing out the sheet music, knowing my arms will be moving around so much. I just get this overwhelming dread that my sleeve will ride up and everyone will see it, and I'll be the center of attention for all the wrong reasons. So, a few times, I’ve just called in and said I had a mild stomach bug or a headache. I feel terrible lying to them, I really do, because they rely on me. But sometimes it just feels easier to stay home where I don't have to constantly monitor my cuffs, you know?
Have you ever had a period of time where you didn't worry about the scar at all?

A period of time where I didn't worry about it at all? Oh, goodness... let me really think about that. You mean like a whole week, or a month, where it just slipped my mind entirely? No. No, I really don't think so. 

I mean, certainly, there are moments, fleeting little moments, where I'm completely absorbed in something else and I suppose I'm not actively thinking about it right that very second. Like last Thursday, for instance. I was trying to reconcile the bank statements for the church—and let me tell you, the bank had made a double charge on our account for the new altar candles, which is just so frustrating because trying to get a real human being on the phone at the branch downtown is like pulling teeth these days, it's all automated menus. Anyway, I was so focused on finding that error, with my reading glasses perched right on the end of my nose, going line by line down the ledger with my yellow highlighter... and for maybe an hour, I wasn't thinking about my wrist. 

But then, of course, I reached across the desk for my calculator, and the sleeve of my cardigan caught on the edge of the desk blotter. It pulled back, and there it was. And just like that, all the worry comes rushing right back in, like a cold draft when someone leaves the front door open. 

So, if you mean a real, proper period of time where I just lived my life and didn't give it a second thought? No, doctor, not at all. It’s just this constant companion, always sitting right there in the back of my mind, waiting for me to remember it again. Even when I'm just sitting in my own living room in the evening, watching Jeopardy with a cup of tea, I'll find myself tugging at my cuffs. It's exhausting, really, just the sheer mental energy it takes to constantly keep track of it, day in and day out. So no, no real break from it, I'm afraid.
How long have you been worrying about the appearance of your wrist scar?

How long? Oh, well... let me think back. It feels like forever, to be perfectly honest with you, but I suppose it hasn't literally been forever. I mean, I got the scar when I was a teenager, actually. I was seventeen, maybe eighteen? It was the summer right after I graduated high school, and my parents had taken me and my younger brother up to this lovely little cabin on Lake Winnipesaukee for a week. I was helping my mother bring in groceries from the station wagon—we had this big, beautiful wood-paneled station wagon back then, the kind you just don't see anymore—and I was carrying this heavy glass jar of sweet pickles. My foot caught on the edge of the porch step, and down I went. The jar shattered, and a piece of the glass caught my wrist. It was quite a fright, lots of blood, and we had to drive all the way into the nearest town to find a doctor to stitch it up. 

But you know, for the longest time after that, for decades really, it was just... a scar. I mean, I went to college, I got married, I started my bookkeeping job, and I never really gave it a second thought. It was just a mark from a clumsy moment when I was young. 

So, when did I start worrying about it like *this*? That's the strange part. It wasn't until... oh, maybe a few years ago? I'd say roughly three or four years ago. I can't quite pinpoint an exact day or a specific event that triggered it. It just sort of... crept up on me. I remember I was at the parish hall, setting up for the annual Christmas bazaar, and someone—I think it was Eleanor, she always means well but she can be a bit blunt—she made a passing comment about it. She just said something like, "Oh, I never noticed that scar on your wrist before, dear." And she didn't mean anything by it, I'm sure she didn't. But for some reason, that comment just stuck with me. It just lodged right in my brain. 

And from that day on, I started looking at it differently. I started noticing how the skin looks a bit raised and shiny compared to the rest of my arm. And then I started wondering if everyone else was noticing it, too, just like Eleanor did. And it just grew from there, you know? It started as just a little seed of self-consciousness, and now it's grown into this... this whole ordeal where I'm constantly pulling down my sleeves and worrying about what people think. So, yes, the scar has been there for over forty years, but this intense worry, this feeling that it's just glaringly obvious to everyone... that's been going on for about three or four years now, I'd say.
Has your worry about the scar ever completely gone away for a period of time, even if it came back later?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, no, it really hasn't ever completely gone away. Not for a day, not for a week, not since this whole ordeal started a few years back. It’s always just hovering right there, simmering in the background. 

And the most frustrating part of it all—and I do try to be rational about this, I really do, because I've always been a very practical person, which you absolutely have to be when you're balancing ledgers all day—is that on some level, I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. I know it's not some gruesome, horrible thing that's going to stop traffic. But my own logic just seems to fly right out the window! 

When I’m out and about, especially in my usual social circles... like at church, or when I'm playing with my Tuesday afternoon bridge group. We've been playing together for, oh, it must be twelve years now, rotating houses every week, and Mary always makes these wonderful little cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off. But even with these women, women I've known and loved for over a decade, I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to my wrist. I’ll be reaching across the card table to play a spade, or passing the collection plate in the pews on Sunday, and I just get this overwhelming sensation that they are all staring right at my arm. It feels like it’s the very first thing they notice about me now. Not my new haircut, not the pie I baked for the potluck, just that shiny, raised mark on my skin. And once that thought gets in my head, I just can't shake it, no matter how much I tell myself I'm being silly, and then I just spend the rest of the afternoon tugging at my sleeves again.
Do you find yourself constantly thinking about the scar, even when you're trying to focus on other things?

Yes, exactly, doctor. That’s just it. Even when I am trying my absolute hardest to focus on something else entirely, it just pushes its way to the front of my mind. 

Like I was just saying about church, or my Tuesday bridge group... I’ll be sitting there, trying my very best to concentrate on counting trumps, or trying to listen to Reverend Thomas—he’s been doing this lovely, very in-depth series on the Psalms lately, which usually I would just soak right up—but my mind just keeps snapping right back to my wrist. It's so terribly distracting. 

Because, well, like I mentioned a moment ago, deep down I really do know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. I try to be logical about it, I really do. But when I’m at church or playing bridge, no matter how hard I try to focus on the cards or the sermon, I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. I sit there completely convinced it’s the first thing they notice about me now, instead of whatever we're actually supposed to be doing or talking about. So instead of focusing on the game and enjoying my friends' company, I'm just obsessing over my arm, completely losing track of the bid. It just takes over everything.
Do you feel that your worry about the scar is interfering with your ability to enjoy social interactions or perform your job as a bookkeeper?

Oh, dear... well, yes. Yes, I suppose it is, and it’s quite embarrassing to admit, to be perfectly honest with you. Because, as I was just saying, I’ve always prided myself on being very reliable. When you do bookkeeping, especially for small local businesses—I handle the accounts for Mr. Henderson’s hardware store and a lovely little florist downtown—you simply have to be punctual with the ledgers and the payroll. People are counting on you. But lately... well, I’ve actually been late turning in some of my bookkeeping work. I'll sit down at my desk at home with my files and my adding machine, fully intending to get the quarterly taxes sorted, but then I catch a glimpse of my arm. And then I start fretting, and I go upstairs to try on different long-sleeved blouses or cardigans to see which one hides it best, or I spend twenty minutes adjusting my cuffs and checking the mirror... and before I know it, half the morning is completely gone and I haven't reconciled a single account. 

And it’s spilling over into my social life and my community activities, too, which just breaks my heart. I’ve been volunteering for years, doctor. I sing in the church choir—second soprano—and we stand right up there in the front of the sanctuary. When you're singing, you have to hold your hymnal or your sheet music up high, which means my wrists are right there on display for the entire congregation to see. So, I’ve actually skipped several choir practices and even a few Sunday services recently. I just call our director, Susan, and tell her I have a scratchy throat or a bit of a cough, which is a terrible fib, but I just can't face standing up there. 

And the community theater, too! I usually volunteer to usher and hand out the playbills for their spring musical. It's always such a wonderful time, greeting all the neighbors as they come into the lobby. But I skipped my theater volunteer commitments this year as well. I just... I get so incredibly caught up in trying to make absolutely sure my wrist won’t be noticed. I'll stand in my living room practicing how to hand out a program without extending my left arm, or trying to figure out how to pin a silk scarf around my wrist so it looks fashionable instead of like I'm hiding something. It just becomes so exhausting and overwhelming that it’s easier to just stay home and skip the whole thing entirely, even though I end up sitting there missing everyone terribly.
Would you say that your worry about the scar is causing you significant distress or interfering with your daily life in a major way?

Well, yes, doctor, absolutely. It's... it's just like I was explaining a moment ago, and I do apologize if I'm repeating myself, but it really is taking a toll. It’s causing me a great deal of distress, more than I ever thought a little mark on my skin could. 

Because, as I mentioned, it really is interfering with my daily life in ways I never would have anticipated. I’ve always been so diligent, so careful with Mr. Henderson's accounts and the florist's payroll, but now I’ve been late turning in my bookkeeping work. I sit there with my adding machine, and instead of tallying up the receipts, I'm just consumed by this worry, checking my sleeves, making sure the cuffs are pulled down just right. It's terribly unprofessional of me, and it weighs on my mind constantly.

And then, of course, there's my volunteering, which has always been such a joy for me. But as I was just saying, I’ve skipped some choir practices and even Sunday services because I just can't bear the thought of holding my hymnal up and exposing my wrist to the whole congregation. And I skipped my theater volunteer commitments for the spring musical, too. I just get so incredibly caught up trying to make absolutely sure my wrist won’t be noticed by anyone... trying to figure out how to hand out playbills without showing my arm, or fussing with scarves to cover it up. It just becomes so overwhelming that I end up staying home, feeling miserable and guilty for letting people down. So, yes, I would say it's causing a very significant disruption in my life. It really is.
Was there something particularly traumatic or upsetting about the experience when you got the scar on your wrist?

Oh, well, no... no, not really. It wasn't traumatic at all, actually. It's quite a silly story, to be perfectly honest. I feel a bit foolish even telling it, considering how much fuss I make over the scar now. But, well, it was just a few months ago, right around the time the weather started turning a bit chilly. I was in my kitchen—I have this lovely little galley kitchen, very efficient, but the oven door is a bit heavy, you see. 

I was baking a batch of my grandmother's ginger snaps for the church bake sale. They’re always a big hit, especially with Reverend Thomas, he just loves them. Anyway, I had just pulled the first tray out—they smelled absolutely divine, all cinnamon and molasses—and I was reaching back in to adjust the rack for the second tray. I must have just been a little clumsy, or maybe I was rushing because the phone was ringing—I think it was my sister, Martha, calling from Ohio, she usually calls on Thursday afternoons—and I just brushed my wrist right against the edge of the hot oven rack. 

It stung, of course, like any burn does, and I ran it under some cold water right away and put a little aloe vera on it. I have a plant right there on the windowsill above the sink for just such occasions. But it really wasn't anything major. I didn't even need to go to the doctor for it or anything like that. It just blistered a tiny bit and then healed over. So, no, there wasn't any big terrible accident or anything traumatic. It was just a silly kitchen mishap, the kind of thing that happens to anyone who bakes. Which makes it all the more ridiculous that I can't seem to stop fixating on it now, doesn't it? It's just a little line from an oven rack, but in my mind... well, you know how it is.
Do you think you would still be this preoccupied with the scar if everyone around you told you it was barely noticeable and didn't bother them at all?

Well, to be perfectly honest with you, doctor... I know for an absolute fact that I would still be just as preoccupied, because, well, that’s exactly what is happening right now. My husband, Arthur—he’s such a dear, patient man, we’ve been married for thirty-eight years this coming May—he tells me all the time that it’s nothing. But it doesn't seem to make a lick of difference to my worrying. 

Every single time before I leave the house, whether it's just to run down to the grocery store for a carton of milk or to drop off the weekly ledgers at Mr. Henderson's hardware store, I go through this whole... ordeal. We have this large oval mirror in our front hallway, it belonged to my mother actually, it has a beautiful carved mahogany frame, and I will stand right there in the entryway and check my wrist in the glass. Not just once, mind you, but a few times. I'll hold my arm up at different angles, stepping back and forth to see how the light from the porch window hits it. 

And if I think it shows even a fraction too much, I’ll run all the way back upstairs and try on different sleeves—maybe a three-quarter length blouse, or a cardigan that I can button tightly at the cuff. Or I'll dig through my jewelry box to find a wide bangle or a chunky bracelet to slide over it, just to make absolutely sure it's covered. 

And then, after all that fussing and changing, I’ll go find Arthur in his armchair in the den, and I'll hold my arm out and ask him if it looks obvious. I'll say, "Arthur, tell me the truth, can you see the mark?" And every single time, bless his heart, he looks at me and says, 'Helen, it's barely there, nobody is going to notice a thing.' He promises me it doesn't bother him one bit. But even with him saying that, looking me right in the eye and assuring me it's fine... I still walk out the front door feeling just as anxious as before. I still tug at my sleeves and fuss with my bracelets the entire car ride. So, yes, even if everyone in the world told me it was unnoticeable, I’m afraid I'd still be standing in front of that hall mirror driving myself absolutely batty over it.
Do you think people are judging you or thinking less of you because of the scar on your wrist?

Well, it’s... it’s a funny thing, doctor, because logically, in my rational mind, I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. I really do try to remind myself of that. I tell myself what Arthur says, that it's just a little mark. But when I'm actually out around people... oh, it's just dreadful, my mind just runs away with me entirely. 

Take my Tuesday afternoon bridge club, for instance. We've been playing together, the four of us—Susan, Margaret, Betty, and myself—for over fifteen years now. We take turns hosting, and when we play, you know, you have to hold your cards up, and your wrists are just right there on display above the felt table for hours on end. I try to keep my sleeves pulled down, but they ride up when you reach across to collect a trick, and I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. I'll be reaching for my iced tea or a little cucumber sandwich, and I can just swear they are all staring right at that spot on my arm instead of looking at the cards. 

And it's the exact same way at church, when I do manage to go. If I'm sitting in the pews or standing around chatting during coffee hour in the fellowship hall... I just have this awful, sinking feeling that it’s the very first thing they notice about me now. They aren't looking at my face, they aren't listening to what I'm saying about the upcoming rummage sale or the flower arrangements, they're just zeroing in on that scar. I know Susan and Betty are dear friends and they wouldn't intentionally think less of me, but I just can't shake this terrible feeling that they're looking at it and wondering what's wrong with me. It just completely takes over my thoughts until I can hardly concentrate on the conversation at all.
Do you believe that people are judging you negatively or thinking less of you because of the scar on your wrist?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor... I suppose I don't really think they are judging me, not in the sense that they think I'm a bad person or anything of that sort. I mean, I've been doing the bookkeeping for Mr. Henderson's hardware store for, oh, it has to be twenty-two years now—I started right around the time my daughter went off to high school—and my ledgers are always meticulous. Not a single penny out of place, Mr. Henderson always says so. And the ladies at the church, well, they know my character inside and out. We’ve organized enough bake sales and charity clothing drives together for them to know exactly who I am and what my values are. 

So, no, when I really sit down and force myself to think about it logically, I don't actually believe they think less of my character or my abilities just because of a silly little burn mark on my arm. I'll sit down at my desk at home with my files and my adding machine, fully intending to get the quarterly taxes sorted, but then I catch a glimpse of my arm. And then I start fretting, and I go upstairs to try on different long-sleeved blouses or cardigans to see which one hides it best, or I spend twenty minutes adjusting my cuffs and checking the mirror... and before I know it, half the morning is completely gone and I haven't reconciled a single account. 

And it’s spilling over into my social life and my community activities, too, which just breaks my heart. I’ve been volunteering for years, doctor. I sing in the church choir—second soprano—and we stand right up there in the front of the sanctuary. When you're singing, you have to hold your hymnal or your sheet music up high, which means my wrists are right there on display for the entire congregation to see. So, I’ve actually skipped several choir practices and even a few Sunday services recently. I just call our director, Susan, and tell her I have a scratchy throat or a bit of a cough, which is a terrible fib, but I just can't face standing up there. 

And the community theater, too! I usually volunteer to usher and hand out the playbills for their spring musical. It's always such a wonderful time, greeting all the neighbors as they come into the lobby. But I skipped my theater volunteer commitments this year as well. I just... I get so incredibly caught up in trying to make absolutely sure my wrist won’t be noticed. I'll stand in my living room practicing how to hand out a program without extending my left arm, or trying to figure out how to pin a silk scarf around my wrist so it looks fashionable instead of like I'm hiding something. It just becomes so exhausting and overwhelming that it’s easier to just stay home and skip the whole thing entirely, even though I end up sitting there missing everyone terribly.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's preoccupation with the scar is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Would you say that your worry about the scar is causing you significant distress or interfering with your daily life in a major way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been late turning in bookkeeping work and have skipped some choir and theater volunteer commitments because I get so caught up trying to make sure my wrist won’t be noticed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worry about the scar is causing significant distress or interfering with daily life in a major way, which directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, doctor, absolutely. It's... it's just like I was explaining a moment ago, and I do apologize if I'm repeating myself, but it really is taking a toll. It’s causing me a great deal of distress, more than I ever thought a little mark on my skin could. 

Because, as I mentioned, it really is interfering with my daily life in ways I never would have anticipated. I’ve always been so diligent, so careful with Mr. Henderson's accounts and the florist's payroll, but now I’ve been late turning in my bookkeeping work. I sit there with my adding machine, and instead of tallying up the receipts, I'm just consumed by this worry, checking my sleeves, making sure the cuffs are pulled down just right. It's terribly unprofessional of me, and it weighs on my mind constantly.

And then, of course, there's my volunteering, which has always been such a joy for me. But as I was just saying, I’ve skipped some choir practices and even Sunday services because I just can't bear the thought of holding my hymnal up and exposing my wrist to the whole congregation. And I skipped my theater volunteer commitments for the spring musical, too. I just get so incredibly caught up trying to make absolutely sure my wrist won’t be noticed by anyone... trying to figure out how to hand out playbills without showing my arm, or fussing with scarves to cover it up. It just becomes so overwhelming that I end up staying home, feeling miserable and guilty for letting people down. So, yes, I would say it's causing a very significant disruption in my life. It really is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's preoccupation with the scar is a result of a traumatic experience associated with the scar
doctor.question: Was there something particularly traumatic or upsetting about the experience when you got the scar on your wrist?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the origin of the scar and if there was a traumatic event associated with it, which is not covered by the symptom profile items (Preoccupation with Appearance, Appearance-Related Repetitive Behaviors, Functional Impairment).

patient.answer:
Oh, well, no... no, not really. It wasn't traumatic at all, actually. It's quite a silly story, to be perfectly honest. I feel a bit foolish even telling it, considering how much fuss I make over the scar now. But, well, it was just a few months ago, right around the time the weather started turning a bit chilly. I was in my kitchen—I have this lovely little galley kitchen, very efficient, but the oven door is a bit heavy, you see. 

I was baking a batch of my grandmother's ginger snaps for the church bake sale. They’re always a big hit, especially with Reverend Thomas, he just loves them. Anyway, I had just pulled the first tray out—they smelled absolutely divine, all cinnamon and molasses—and I was reaching back in to adjust the rack for the second tray. I must have just been a little clumsy, or maybe I was rushing because the phone was ringing—I think it was my sister, Martha, calling from Ohio, she usually calls on Thursday afternoons—and I just brushed my wrist right against the edge of the hot oven rack. 

It stung, of course, like any burn does, and I ran it under some cold water right away and put a little aloe vera on it. I have a plant right there on the windowsill above the sink for just such occasions. But it really wasn't anything major. I didn't even need to go to the doctor for it or anything like that. It just blistered a tiny bit and then healed over. So, no, there wasn't any big terrible accident or anything traumatic. It was just a silly kitchen mishap, the kind of thing that happens to anyone who bakes. Which makes it all the more ridiculous that I can't seem to stop fixating on it now, doesn't it? It's just a little line from an oven rack, but in my mind... well, you know how it is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's preoccupation with the scar is a result of a body dysmorphic disorder or a persistent personality trait
doctor.question: Do you think you would still be this preoccupied with the scar if everyone around you told you it was barely noticeable and didn't bother them at all?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: Before I leave the house, I’ll check my wrist in the hall mirror a few times, try different sleeves or a bracelet to cover it, and sometimes ask my husband if it looks obvious, even though he always says it’s barely there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if reassurance from others (that the scar is barely noticeable) would stop her preoccupation. The patient's manifestation for S068 perfectly addresses this, as she asks her husband for reassurance and he tells her it's 'barely there', yet she continues her repetitive checking and covering behaviors.

patient.answer:
Well, to be perfectly honest with you, doctor... I know for an absolute fact that I would still be just as preoccupied, because, well, that’s exactly what is happening right now. My husband, Arthur—he’s such a dear, patient man, we’ve been married for thirty-eight years this coming May—he tells me all the time that it’s nothing. But it doesn't seem to make a lick of difference to my worrying. 

Every single time before I leave the house, whether it's just to run down to the grocery store for a carton of milk or to drop off the weekly ledgers at Mr. Henderson's hardware store, I go through this whole... ordeal. We have this large oval mirror in our front hallway, it belonged to my mother actually, it has a beautiful carved mahogany frame, and I will stand right there in the entryway and check my wrist in the glass. Not just once, mind you, but a few times. I'll hold my arm up at different angles, stepping back and forth to see how the light from the porch window hits it. 

And if I think it shows even a fraction too much, I’ll run all the way back upstairs and try on different sleeves—maybe a three-quarter length blouse, or a cardigan that I can button tightly at the cuff. Or I'll dig through my jewelry box to find a wide bangle or a chunky bracelet to slide over it, just to make absolutely sure it's covered. 

And then, after all that fussing and changing, I’ll go find Arthur in his armchair in the den, and I'll hold my arm out and ask him if it looks obvious. I'll say, "Arthur, tell me the truth, can you see the mark?" And every single time, bless his heart, he looks at me and says, 'Helen, it's barely there, nobody is going to notice a thing.' He promises me it doesn't bother him one bit. But even with him saying that, looking me right in the eye and assuring me it's fine... I still walk out the front door feeling just as anxious as before. I still tug at my sleeves and fuss with my bracelets the entire car ride. So, yes, even if everyone in the world told me it was unnoticeable, I’m afraid I'd still be standing in front of that hall mirror driving myself absolutely batty over it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's preoccupation with the scar is driven by a fear of negative evaluation by others

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me, but when I’m at church or bridge I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.

This relates directly to her preoccupation with the appearance of the scar and her feeling that everyone's eyes go right to it (perceived defect not observable/slight to others), which matches symptom S067.

patient.answer:
Well, it’s... it’s a funny thing, doctor, because logically, in my rational mind, I know the scar on my wrist is probably not as bad as it looks to me. I really do try to remind myself of that. I tell myself what Arthur says, that it's just a little mark. But when I'm actually out around people... oh, it's just dreadful, my mind just runs away with me entirely. 

Take my Tuesday afternoon bridge club, for instance. We've been playing together, the four of us—Susan, Margaret, Betty, and myself—for over fifteen years now. We take turns hosting, and when we play, you know, you have to hold your cards up, and your wrists are just right there on display above the felt table for hours on end. I try to keep my sleeves pulled down, but they ride up when you reach across to collect a trick, and I just keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. I'll be reaching for my iced tea or a little cucumber sandwich, and I can just swear they are all staring right at that spot on my arm instead of looking at the cards. 

And it's the exact same way at church, when I do manage to go. If I'm sitting in the pews or standing around chatting during coffee hour in the fellowship hall... I just have this awful, sinking feeling that it’s the very first thing they notice about me now. They aren't looking at my face, they aren't listening to what I'm saying about the upcoming rummage sale or the flower arrangements, they're just zeroing in on that scar. I know Susan and Betty are dear friends and they wouldn't intentionally think less of me, but I just can't shake this terrible feeling that they're looking at it and wondering what's wrong with me. It just completely takes over my thoughts until I can hardly concentrate on the conversation at all.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's preoccupation with the scar is driven by a fear of negative evaluation by others
doctor.question: Do you believe that people are judging you negatively or thinking less of you because of the scar on your wrist?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's belief regarding others judging them negatively (fear of negative evaluation or insight/delusional beliefs), which is not covered by the remaining symptom profile (Functional Impairment).

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor... I suppose I don't really think they are judging me, not in the sense that they think I'm a bad person or anything of that sort. I mean, I've been doing the bookkeeping for Mr. Henderson's hardware store for, oh, it has to be twenty-two years now—I started right around the time my daughter went off to high school—and my ledgers are always meticulous. Not a single penny out of place, Mr. Henderson always says so. And the ladies at the church, well, they know my character inside and out. We’ve organized enough bake sales and charity clothing drives together for them to know exactly who I am and what my values are. 

So, no, when I really sit down and force myself to think about it logically, I don't actually believe they think less of my character or my abilities just because of a silly little burn mark on my arm. It’s more just... well, it’s not judgment so much as it is this overwhelming, exhausting fear that it’s simply all they can focus on when they look at me. Like it's an awful eyesore that they just can't politely ignore. 

But as for them actually judging me negatively or thinking I'm somehow lesser? No, I don't have any real reason to think that. Arthur always tells me, 'Helen, these people love you, they couldn't care less about a mark on your wrist.' And I know he's right. I really, truly do. It's just my own mind playing tricks on me, making me feel so terribly exposed and self-conscious, even though I know perfectly well that Susan and Betty aren't sitting there at the bridge table evaluating my worth as a human being over a kitchen mishap. So, no, I don't think they're judging me. It's just me judging myself, I suppose.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's preoccupation with the scar is driven by a fear of negative evaluation by others
doctor.question: Do you believe that the reason you're so concerned about the scar is because you think others will evaluate you negatively if they see it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the concern is driven by a fear of negative evaluation by others (which helps differentiate BDD from Social Anxiety Disorder), but my symptom profile only covers preoccupation with appearance, repetitive behaviors, and functional impairment. It does not contain a specific item for fear of negative evaluation.

patient.answer:
Well, no... no, I really don't think that's it. I mean, I know we were just talking about this, and I really don't believe people are evaluating me negatively at all. Honestly, if people in this town were going to evaluate me, they’ve had plenty of other opportunities over the years! 

Take the spring gala at the church, for example. I’ve organized the silent auction for the past, oh, it must be six years now, coordinating with all the merchants down on Main Street to get donations, making sure the bid sheets are printed up nicely. And they all know I do a wonderful job, everything is always perfectly accounted for. My bookkeeping at Mr. Henderson's is the same way. So they certainly aren't going to suddenly think I'm incompetent or evaluate me poorly as a person just because I have a blemish on my arm. 

It’s so frustrating, really, because Arthur asks me the exact same thing. He’ll sit there with his morning newspaper and his coffee, watching me fuss with my cuffs, and he'll say, "Helen, who exactly are you worried is going to grade you on this?" And I always tell him, "Nobody, Arthur!" Because I know they aren't. I just... I honestly don't know why I get in such a state about it. I just look at it and it bothers me so much, it just feels so glaring and out of place to me. I just want to look put together, you know? 

But as for worrying about other people evaluating me negatively? No, I really don't think that's the reason at all. I don't have any reason to think they'd do that. I wish I could give you a better explanation for why it upsets me so much, doctor, I really do, because it drives me just as crazy as it drives Arthur! But no, it's not because I think they're evaluating me.
